analysis.one_liner: Caps the combined federal, state, and local taxes any individual pays at half their income.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee until the Congress ended, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The Max Tax Act would have created an alternative cap on taxes for individuals: add up every tax a person pays in a year — federal income tax, payroll taxes, state and local income, sales, and property taxes, even excise taxes like gasoline, cigarette, and telephone taxes — and if that total exceeded 50% of the person's adjusted gross income, their federal tax bill would be reduced so the total never topped half their income. The cap applied only to individuals, not corporations. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never advanced: no hearing, no markup, no vote, and not a single cosponsor joined before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households whose combined tax burden approaches or exceeds 50% of their income. Most working families pay well under 50% of their income in combined federal, state, and local taxes, so the cap would rarely bind for them; it would mainly cut bills for top earners facing the highest federal rates plus high state taxes, and for very large estates (estate and gift taxes are on the counted list).

how_it_helps.text: Creates an alternative maximum tax: no individual's combined federal, state, and local taxes could exceed 50% of adjusted gross income, with federal tax reduced to make up the difference.

The list of taxes counted toward the cap is sweeping — income, payroll, self-employment, sales, property, estate, gift, gasoline, cigarette, telephone, utility, hotel, and ACA-related taxes — so nearly every tax a household pays counts toward the 50% ceiling.
For a top earner in a high-tax state whose combined rate would otherwise exceed 50%, the provision converts much of their state and local tax burden into a lower federal bill.
The cap excludes corporations, so its benefits flow entirely to non-corporate taxpayers — in practice, the households with the largest tax bills.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally: the revenue the government would have collected from high earners above the 50% cap would have to be made up through other taxes, borrowing, or spending cuts. State and local tax collections would continue, but the federal treasury would absorb the overage.

drawbacks.text: The cap would sharply reduce federal revenue from the highest earners, shifting the cost to other taxpayers, future borrowing, or program cuts.

Because state and local taxes count toward the federal cap, residents of high-tax states would effectively have the federal government subsidize their state and local tax bills — a design that favors taxpayers in high-tax states.
The provision would add a second, parallel tax calculation requiring individuals to tally dozens of different taxes each year, a substantial recordkeeping and compliance burden.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cap looks like a broad taxpayer protection, but it is designed so it almost never helps ordinary families — most pay far less than half their income in all taxes combined — while delivering large cuts to those with the biggest bills. The cost is real: significant lost federal revenue and a more complicated tax code. A cap pitched at everyone but written to bind only at the top delivers its benefits narrow and deep.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Jolly introduced the bill on April 29, 2014, and it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over its lifetime.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2015, and the bill expired in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, high earners gained nothing — but no revenue was lost either. The outcome mostly preserved the existing tax structure, and spared the federal treasury the revenue loss the cap would have caused.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The federal treasury; the bill went nowhere

for.name: Rep. David Jolly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Max Tax Act and referred it to Ways and Means; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing or markup — letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other member took a public position; the only recorded actions were one sponsor and one committee referral.

industries.note: The 50% cap on all taxes combined would bind mainly for top earners and large estates, cutting their federal bills. The revenue forgone would fall on other taxpayers or the deficit.
State and local taxes would still be collected, but the federal cap would subsidize residents' state and local bills, creating pressure toward lower state taxes and adding federal cost.
